title: Is It Worth Your Budget? Classroom Libraries
author: RatedEd
summary: RatedEd runs the actual cost-per-book math on seven common channels teachers use to stock a 200-book classroom library, from First Book (roughly $70-$100 total, but eligibility-gated) to retail purchase ($1,500-plus, never a bulk strategy). The piece's central argument is that cheap-book advice is incomplete unless it accounts for time cost, illustrated by the line that a channel saving $1.10 per book but costing six hours of sorting is really 'a second job that pays about $37 an hour in book credit.' It flags an equity problem in Scholastic Book Clubs points, which reward high-poverty classrooms the least because they depend on family purchasing power. The recommended strategy is a blend: check First Book eligibility first, run Scholastic Clubs passively all year, hit one warehouse or library sale for volume, and reserve ThriftBooks or retail only for specific must-have titles.
points: RatedEd's central point reframes 'cheap' as incomplete without a time cost: 'a channel that saves you $1.10 per book and costs six hours of sorting is not a deal. It is a second job that pays about $37 an hour in book credit.'

First Book's National Book Bank is rated the best value at roughly $70-$100 for 200 books, but is gated by school/program eligibility for kids in need, which many teachers wrongly assume excludes them.
Scholastic Book Clubs points are flagged as a hidden equity problem: because rewards are funded by family orders, high-poverty classrooms that need books most earn the fewest free books.

The recommended strategy blends channels by purpose: First Book for baseline eligibility, Scholastic Clubs running passively all year, one warehouse or library sale for bulk volume, and ThriftBooks/retail reserved only for specific must-have titles.
quotes: Every classroom library article gives you the same list of places to get cheap books. None of them do the math.
A channel that saves you $1.10 per book and costs six hours of sorting is not a deal. It is a second job that pays about $37 an hour in book credit.
In a high-poverty building this channel produces very little, which is a real equity problem worth naming: the classrooms that need books most earn the fewest points.
The honest strategy for most teachers is a blend: check First Book eligibility first, run Scholastic Clubs all year in the background, hit one warehouse sale or library sale for volume.
Two hundred books does not just cost money. It costs sorting, leveling if you level, labeling, shelving, and a checkout system you will abandon by November.
Recruit students for the sorting, because they are better at knowing which books their classmates will pick up than you are, and it gives them ownership of the shelf.
